_about: The page's explanations in the gabe-lens voice, for the operator's calibrated suit (Sequential-Procedural: a thing is a sequence of steps and what breaks when one is skipped; see ~/.claude/gabe-lens-profile.md) - D-079, answering L-31. AUTHORED text: for each of the ten patterns a pain, one analogy (a process) with where it stops, the steps of how the defect happens (time top to bottom, the step where it goes wrong marked), a box (does, does not do, decides when), the cost (to solve, if not) and a handle; for each of the 53 decisions a pain, one analogy with where it stops, the cost and a handle. A number is a {token} gen-legibility-review.mjs fills from the data (the words sweep reaches this file too: a typed digit or number word stops the build); no id, path, code or symbol stands here. `kind` picks the pain's icon and `process` the analogy's icon (icons.json); `meter` says which real count the pain's meter draws (a measured check before and now, a count of a total, a tally, or how often the pattern came up); `size` is the cost to solve (small, medium or large) where the generator cannot derive it, and `sizeWhy` says in a few words what the size is counted in; `marks` says for each option of a look whether picking it gains, costs, both or is neutral.

pain.text: You point at a rate limit refusal on {ep} to learn why that request ended, and the hover defines every refusal there is. You point at the next refusal and read the same words, so you cannot tell them apart.

like.analogy: It is like a pharmacy that sticks the same leaflet about the whole drug family on every bottle and never prints the dose, so bottles of different strength look alike on the counter.
like.stops: It stops being true where the leaflet is wanted, because what a kind means still has to be written once, in a key.

steps.t: You point at the first refusal.
The hover opens and defines what every refusal is.
You point at the next refusal.
The same hover opens, word for word.
You compare them from memory and cannot tell which is which.

box.does: Opens every item's hover with what its kind is.
box.doesNot: Say what this item checks, what comes before it or what it gives.
box.decidesWhen: It bites whenever items of one kind sit side by side and you need the difference.

cost.toSolve: Landing both is a pass over the audit script that counts these defects, plus a few short written rules, and every count it raises needs your look before anything is fixed.
cost.ifNot: The next page an agent builds repeats the definition on every item again, as this page did {repeatLine_before} times at the start and still does {repeatLine_now} times.
cost.sizeWhy: a pass over one script and a few short rules

P1.handle: Dose on the bottle, leaflet in the drawer.

pain.text: You point at an item to learn about the code, and the hover opens with a line about where the page took a colour or an icon from. At the start {pageTalk_before} hovers talked about the page or the tool that reads the code, and {pageTalk_now} still do.

like.analogy: It is like an airport announcement that begins with how the loudspeaker works, so the gate and the boarding time you came for arrive late or never.
like.stops: It stops being true where the speaker is the subject, because a panel about the code tool on purpose may talk about it.

steps.t: You point at an item to learn something about the code.
The hover opens with a line about how the page drew it.
You read it, looking for a fact about the code.
The fact is further down, or it is not there.

box.does: Tells you where the page took a colour or an icon, or what the code tool could not read.
box.doesNot: Tell you anything about the code, which is what you came to read.
box.decidesWhen: It bites whenever a fact about how the page was built sits where a fact about the code should be.

cost.toSolve: Landing both is a pass over the audit script, a stop list in each page generator, the program that builds a page, and one written rule, with room for panels that talk about the tool.
cost.ifNot: Every new page brings its own sentences about itself, and {pageTalk_now} hovers talk about the page today.
cost.sizeWhy: a pass over the audit script and a stop list in each generator

P2.handle: Announce the gate, not the loudspeaker.

pain.text: You scan a row on {ep} and some of its small labels are bare words, with no icon and no kind, so you stop at each one to ask what it is. The count of items without an icon was {bare_before} at the start and is {bare_now} now.

like.analogy: It is like a hospital ward where some patients wear no wristband, so every nurse stops at the bed to ask who this is before doing anything.
like.stops: It stops being true where a wristband is cheap, because an icon on every label can crowd a dense row.

steps.t: You scan a row of small labels.
Some wear an icon and some are only a word.
You stop at a bare word and ask what kind of thing it is.
You open it or ask, and only then read on.

box.does: Draws an item as a bare word, with no kind and no role.
box.doesNot: Say what the item is or what it does.
box.decidesWhen: It bites when an item is a kind the page has no mark for.

cost.toSolve: Landing both is a pass over the audit script that counts bare items, plus one written rule, and the count waits on your ruling about gate icons.
cost.ifNot: New items keep arriving as bare words, {bare_now} still wear no icon, and you keep asking what each one is.
cost.sizeWhy: a pass over the audit script and one rule

pain.text: You read a condition on {ep} and cannot tell which function checks it, or you see a refresh and not what it fetches. The page drew one end of the link, so every half link is a question you have to go and answer yourself.

like.analogy: It is like a booking form for a train ticket that prints the station you leave from and not the one you reach, so you still have to ask where it goes.
like.stops: It stops being true where a ticket is one object, because here the ends are separate records the page could have joined.

steps.t: The record joins a function to its condition.
The page draws the condition and leaves the function out.
You read the condition and look for who checks it.
You find a file name and a line number, and no function.
You go and ask, or open the code.

box.does: Draws one end of a link and leaves the other end to the record behind it.
box.doesNot: Name the function, the table or the fetch at the other end.
box.decidesWhen: It bites whenever a record joins a pair of things and the page shows only one.

cost.toSolve: Landing both is a check in each page generator, the program that builds a page, that stops the build, plus one written rule, and each generator must first say which records join a pair of things.
cost.ifNot: Pages keep drawing half a link, and you keep asking checked where, or fetched from what.
cost.sizeWhy: a check in each page generator that stops the build

pain.text: You read down the table that lays a request out step by step on {ep}, where a column holds no step, a mark has no key, and a long name breaks inside a word. At the start {midWord_before} words broke in the middle.

like.analogy: It is like a bus timetable that prints a fare in the column of departure times and cuts a station name in half at the paper's edge.
like.stops: It stops being true where paper is fixed, because a page can be made wider, and that width is the cost the fix pays.

steps.t: You read down a column of steps in time order.
One column holds a fact with no time in it.
You take it for one more step and read it as one.
A name inside it breaks mid-word and stops your reading.
You work out what the column is from its neighbours.

box.does: Puts a timeless fact in a timeline, or leaves a mark without its key.
box.doesNot: Tell you which columns are steps or what a mark means.
box.decidesWhen: It bites when a column's kind or a mark's meaning lives only in a hover.

cost.toSolve: Landing both is new checks in the gate that runs before a publish, each with a test case, plus one written rule, and a failing check can hold back a page you want.
cost.ifNot: Each new surface brings its own cut words and unmarked columns, and you find them by eye.
cost.sizeWhy: new checks in the render gate that holds back a publish

P5.handle: Keep fares out of the timetable.

pain.text: You look on {ep} for the piece of the web app that sends the request and find it under several names, so you take each name for a different thing. Elsewhere one word stands for a kind and for a lifetime, so you take them for one.

like.stops: It stops being true where a clerk can see the parcel, because a page has only words, and telling concepts apart from words alone is a guess.

steps.t: You see a name for something in one view.
In another view the same thing has another name.
You take the second name for a second thing.
Or one word stands for a kind and a lifetime and you take them for one.

pain.text: You read a label on {ep} and meet a condition spelled as the code spells it, or a library's error name where a reason belongs. You are a programmer and still have to decode it, and the text of an error is often not the message at all.

steps.t: The code holds a condition as an expression.
The page copies the expression onto a label.
You read it and have to decode what it means.
You are not sure the expression is the message at all.
You open the code to be sure.

box.does: Shows an expression as the code spells it.
box.doesNot: Say in words what the expression means.
box.decidesWhen: It bites when the page copies a value out of the code without turning it into a sentence.

cost.toSolve: Landing both is a pass over the audit script that counts raw words on labels, plus one written rule, and each hit needs your look.
cost.ifNot: Labels keep showing the code's spelling, as {machineWords_before} did at the start, and you keep decoding it.

pain.text: You read a label on {ep} that says no headers were sent, or that a test proves an ending, when the rule behind it never read the headers or only fits the ending. You trust the label, and the page tells you something that is not true.

like.analogy: It is like a bank statement headed balance whose figure is only the total of deposits, so the teller trusts the heading and signs.
like.stops: It stops being true where the bank states its rule, because a page's label is held to its rule only where the generator states both.

steps.t: The generator computes a number by one rule.
The page prints the number under a label.
The label says more than the rule counts.
You read the label literally and trust it.
You act on a fact that is looser than it sounds.

box.does: Prints a label stronger than the rule behind it, or shows unknown as none.
box.doesNot: Say what the rule really counts.
box.decidesWhen: It bites when a label is typed into a template and does not come from the rule.

cost.toSolve: Landing both is a check in each page generator that stops the build, plus one clause in the execution contract every skill follows.
cost.ifNot: Labels keep promising more than their rule counts, and a bare zero keeps hiding that nobody looked.
cost.sizeWhy: a check in each generator and a clause that reaches every skill

steps.t: The page draws every element at once in a dense table.

box.does: Draws many elements at once before one has been decided alone.
box.doesNot: Give you one element, with its parts and its controls, to look at.

meter.noun: endpoints whose table runs past its box

pain.text: Names now stay whole, so on {nScroll} of {nEp} endpoints the table that lays a request out step by step is wider than its box and you scroll sideways. You open an endpoint and the columns near the answer are already off the screen.

like.analogy: It is like a shirt back from the laundry, which can arrive already folded to fit the drawer or loose, folded only when you reach for it.
like.stops: It stops being true where a folded shirt is still a shirt, because a fitted table is narrowed or wrapped, so something you read whole is squeezed.

cost.toSolve: One click of yours, since opening fitted changes a default on the {nScroll} endpoints that overflow and leaves the others as they are.
cost.ifNot: On {nScroll} of {nEp} endpoints you keep scrolling sideways, one click away from fitting.
cost.sizeWhy: one click of yours and nothing in the suite changes

R-11.handle: Fold it for the drawer, or leave it loose.

meter.noun: kinds whose bench look the table's labels cannot use yet

pain.text: On {ep} the bench draws the function that does the work as a block, while the table draws the same function as a small label. A look you decide on the bench never reaches the table, so the look you chose is not the one you read.

like.analogy: It is like approving a prototype on the workshop bench and then running the production line from a different drawing, so the thing you approved is not the thing that ships.
like.stops: It stops being true where a prototype is a one-off, because here a bench look can become the table's look the day you rule one.

cost.toSolve: Waiting costs nothing and builds the new cell option once you rule a kind's look, while building it now adds one more cell option on looks that are only my picks.
cost.ifNot: A look decided on the bench keeps not reaching the table, and you keep reading different looks for one function.
cost.sizeWhy: one more cell option in the table if built now, nothing if it waits

EX-5.handle: Approve the sample before you tool the line.
